card.name: Tatsia
card.tagline: A Cypriot trick dance balancing glasses of wine inside a spinning wooden sieve.
card.profile: Tatsia is a traditional Cypriot dance of skill and agility named after the local dialect word for a sieve (τατσιά). Performed historically by men as a competitive display or to impress onlookers, the dancer balances a glass of wine inside the rim of a hand-held wooden sieve while executing fast, continuous arm loops and spinning sequences. An assistant places wine filled to mid-glass inside the sieve before the dancer launches into figure-eight trajectory patterns around the body, overhead, and under the armpits. Advanced variations involve changing hands mid-air, stacking multiple glasses, or performing the entire sequence kneeling.
card.insight: A Cypriot solo challenge dance where men spin a wooden flour sieve—carrying up to three glasses of wine—around their bodies and under their armpits without spilling a drop.
card.profile_long:
Tatsia origins and history trace back to traditional male social gatherings in Cyprus, where the dance developed as a physical test of agility, stamina, and hand control. Named directly after the Cypriot dialect word for a sieve—τατσιά—the dance transformed an everyday agricultural household tool into a dramatic prop for bravado and competitive courtship. Dancers sought to outdo one another by performing complex geometric patterns with the sieve while keeping wine glasses balanced inside, demonstrating total mastery over centrifugal motion.

How it is danced hinges on absolute continuous movement paired with precise upper-body control and traditional Cypriot footwork. The dancer holds the sieve with four fingers placed inside the top rim and the thumb resting on the outside edge. An assistant or the dancer places a glass filled with wine—never exceeding the middle of the glass—onto the inside bottom rim. The performer then drives the sieve through fluid, sweeping loops around the torso and head. Key figures include the Basic 8, where the hand twists inward to pass the sieve under the armpit before looping over the head, and the Reverse 8, which reverses the circular sweep. Intermediate transfers like the Change and Reverse Change require shifting the sieve behind the back or overhead from hand to hand while maintaining rotational momentum.

Music and instruments follow standard Cypriot folk dance accompaniment, providing a rhythmic framework for the dancer's footwork and manual acrobatics. The rhythm must maintain a precise tempo, as any sudden change in pace or abrupt jerk of the arm breaks the centrifugal balance, sending the glass off the surface or spilling the wine.

Costume and setting are rooted in rural Cypriot tradition, originally performed in village squares, coffee houses, or wedding celebrations. The central visual element is the prop itself: a wooden flour sieve containing one or more wine glasses. To increase difficulty, expert dancers use larger sieves, inserting a small wooden platform across three base glasses to stack additional filled glasses on top.

Occasions and meaning center on athletic competition, showmanship, and entertainment. Created by Cypriot men as a form of friendly rivalry, the dance serves as a public demonstration of grace under pressure, endurance, and immaculate control.

sections.origins_and_history: Tatsia takes its name from τατσιά, the Cypriot dialect word for a sieve. It was created by men in Cyprus as a form of athletic competition and showcase, serving as a display of dexterity and stamina intended to impress onlookers and showcase physical mastery.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dancer holds a sieve with four main fingers on the top of the inside perimeter and the thumb on the outside perimeter. A glass of wine, filled no higher than the middle, is placed on the bottom inside rim. The dancer maintains continuous, non-stop motion to prevent the glass from falling or spilling. Basic movement patterns include the 8, where the wrist twists inward as the body leans to pass the sieve beneath the armpit before drawing a half circle overhead; the Reverse 8, starting with a large lateral circle above the head before folding inward under the armpit; and hand transfers including the Change overhead and the Reverse Change behind the back during a body spin. Dancers must possess high stamina, absolute control over their hands, and mastery of traditional footwork.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed in strict time to rhythmic Cypriot folk music. Maintaining a steady tempo is critical, as the dancer relies on consistent rhythmic timing to execute continuous centrifugal sweeps without disturbing the balanced wine glasses.
sections.costume_and_setting: Tatsia is performed with a traditional wooden sieve (tatsia) and wine glasses filled to mid-level. For advanced demonstrations, dancers use a larger sieve fitted with a small piece of wooden planking laid across three base glasses to create an elevated platform for additional glasses. The glasses must never touch the top perimeter of the sieve.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically performed by men as a competitive exhibition or courtship display, Tatsia serves as a test of skill, balance, and poise. It turns common domestic objects into a dramatic display of physical mastery.
sections.regional_variants: Variants of difficulty depend on posture and props rather than geography: dancers perform standard sequences or expert combinations while sitting on one knee, or stack multiple tiers of glasses using auxiliary wooden boards.
sections.lineage: Categorised as a Greek folk dance variant from the island of Cyprus, specifically defined as an object-balancing male solo challenge dance.

basic_steps: Grip the top perimeter of the sieve with four fingers inside and the thumb on the outside.
Execute the Basic 8 by leaning forward, twisting the wrist inward to pass the sieve under the armpit, and extending upward into a high overhead arc.
Execute the Reverse 8 by raising the arm in a broad lateral circle overhead, then folding the elbow inward to pass under the armpit.
Perform the Change by grabbing the sieve overhead with the opposite hand at the peak of the 8 arc, continuing directly into a Reverse 8.
Perform the Reverse Change by sweeping the sieve behind the back during a torso spin and transferring hands behind the body.
teaching.rhythm: Steady rhythmic meter aligned with traditional Cypriot folk dance.
teaching.formation: Solo performance, often accompanied by an assistant who places or adjusts the glasses.
teaching.level_notes: Requires high manual control, wrist flexibility, continuous fluid movement, and stamina. Advanced variations involve kneeling or multi-glass stacking.

episode_brief.title_hook: Balancing Wine on a Spinning Sieve
episode_brief.logline: A Cypriot dancer tests speed, stamina, and centrifugal force by sweeping a wine-laden wooden sieve around his body without spilling a drop.
beats: An assistant carefully places a glass half-full of wine inside the rim of a wooden sieve.
The dancer grips the sieve rim and initiates a smooth, continuous Basic 8 trajectory.
The sieve sweeps under the armpit and arcs high overhead in a unbroken fluid motion.
The dancer transitions into a Reverse Change, spinning on axis while swapping hands behind his back.
The performance culminates with the dancer dropping to one knee while continuing overhead figure-eight patterns.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the correct sieve grip and basic armpit pass without props.
drills: Practice four-finger inside grip with thumb outside on an empty sieve frame.
Execute slow-motion armpit passes while leaning the torso forward.
Trace overhead half-circles maintaining constant upward tilt of the sieve base.

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute full figure-eight loops and overhead hand transfers.
drills: Connect the lower armpit loop continuously with the upper overhead arc in the Basic 8.
Practice the Change by transferring the prop hand-to-hand at the highest point of the overhead arc.
Perform the Reverse 8 sequence smoothly without stopping momentum.

lesson_ladder.goal: Perform complex combinations with a filled wine glass and kneeling variations.
drills: Perform the Basic Rotation sequence (Basic 8 - Change - Reverse 8 - Reverse Change - Basic 8) with an empty glass.
Add a half-filled water glass and execute full figure-eight patterns.
Perform figure-eight variations while sitting on one knee.
